beats.o71: இப்போது வாதம். ஒன்று. மெல்லிய மார்ஜினில் தவறுக்கு இடம் குறைவு. இரண்டு. நிர்வாகம் ஆசையை எதிர்க்கும் வரைதான் ஒப்பந்தம். ஒரு பேராசை பாஸ், முடிந்தது. மூன்று. குறைந்த ஷேர் விலை மோசமான விலையில் கையகப்படுத்தலை அழைக்கலாம் என்று Sleep-ஏ எச்சரித்தார். நான்கு. இந்தக் கலாச்சாரத்தைப் பின்னால் கட்டுவது கடினம். பெரும்பாலும் முதல் நாளிலிருந்தே இருக்க வேண்டும்.
beats.o72: எங்கள் தீர்ப்பு. Costco மோட், அளவுப் பலனைப் பகிர்வது, மார்க்அப் ரகசியமாக மாறாது என்று நம்பும் வாடிக்கையாளர். பெரிய ஆபத்து, கொஞ்சம் அதிகம் எடுக்கும் ஆசை. நிலை? Nomad-இன் மிகப் பெரிய பந்தயம், பார்ட்னர்ஷிப் மூடும்போதும் கையில்.
beats.o80: சிறந்த மதிப்பு தருவதாகச் சொல்லும் எந்த இந்திய கம்பெனிக்கும், மூன்று கேள்விகள்.
beats.o81: ஒன்று. செலவு குறையும்போது விலையும் குறைகிறதா? இரண்டு. கம்பெனி வைக்கும் ஒவ்வொரு ரூபாய்க்கும் வாடிக்கையாளர் எவ்வளவு சேமிக்கிறார்? மூன்று. எதிர்பாராத லாபம் வந்தால், கொஞ்சம் வாடிக்கையாளருக்குத் திருப்புமா?
beats.o82: எந்த இந்திய கம்பெனியையும் சொல்லவில்லை. நீங்களே விசாரியுங்கள்.
beats.o83: நண்பனுக்கு ஒரு வரி. சேமிப்பைப் பகிரும் கடை, வாடிக்கையாளரை வைத்துக்கொள்ளும்.
beats.o84: ஒவ்வொரு தடயமும் Nick Sleep பார்ட்னர்களுக்கு எழுதிய கடிதங்களிலிருந்து. ஆதாரங்கள் டிஸ்க்ரிப்ஷனில்.
beats.o85: அடுத்த கேஸ். நாற்பது வருடம் விலை அதிகம் போல் தெரிந்த ஒரு கடைச் சங்கிலி, புத்திசாலி முதலீட்டாளர்கள் சீக்கிரமே விற்றார்கள். வளரும் மோட்டை எப்படி மதிப்பிடுவது? கேஸ் ஃபைல் ஒன்பது. சப்ஸ்க்ரைப் பண்ணுங்கள்.

o00.say: A buyer at Costco has found a steal. Two million pairs of designer jeans. Shipped out into international waters, and brought back in, for about twenty two dollars a pair, all in. That's ten dollars below the price Costco used to sell them at. And half what most other stores pay.

o01.say: Costco's usual markup is about fourteen percent. Sell at the old price instead, and that's a fifty percent markup. One buyer said, let's take the bigger margin this time. No one would know.

o02.say: The founder, Jim Sinegal, said no. Fourteen percent, as always. His reason? If I let you do it this time, you will do it again.

o03.say: This is the case of Costco. Why would a company refuse easy profit? Is that a moat, or just charity? And why did a famous fund manager make it his largest holding?

o11.say: Our detective here is Nick Sleep, who ran the Nomad Investment Partnership with Qais Zakaria. In their letter for two thousand two, they explained how Costco works. You pay a membership fee, then forty five dollars, just to get in for a year.

o12.say: In return, Costco marks up everything by a fixed amount. About fourteen percent on brands, fifteen on its own label. The fee is almost all profit. The goods are sold at just above cost. Sleep called it a very simple and honest deal with the customer.

o13.say: Compare that with most shops. They push prices up and down to pull in traffic. Is a bottle of shampoo worth two dollars, if it's sometimes one dollar with a coupon? At Costco, Sleep wrote, the customer knows the price is fourteen or fifteen percent above wholesale. Period.

o14.say: That's why the jeans mattered so much. One secret markup, and the deal is broken. Costco's own managers described the strategy as easy to understand, and hard to operate.

o21.say: So how do you make money at such tiny margins? Sleep found three things. First, costs are low. Very low. Costco measures its costs in basis points. That's hundredths of a percent.

o22.say: Second, the cheapest possible buying. A store carries only about four thousand products. And each of those spots goes to whichever supplier offers customers the best value. Costco even told suppliers that any vendor who doesn't always quote its lowest price, will be permanently dropped. Sleep's reaction? Grief. One strike and you're out.

o23.say: Compare that with a normal supermarket. It acts like a landlord, renting shelf space to the highest bidding supplier. Sleep put it simply. Many supermarkets make their money from buying from the supplier. Costco makes money from selling to the consumer.

o24.say: And third, huge sales. Costco's sales per square foot ran about fifty percent above its closest rival, Wal-Mart's Sam's Club.

o31.say: Here's the real secret. When Costco gets bigger and buys cheaper, it doesn't keep the savings. It cuts prices. Lower prices bring more shoppers. More shoppers mean bigger volumes. Bigger volumes mean cheaper buying. And round again. Even the shoppers at the oldest stores benefit, every time a new one opens.

o32.say: Sleep had a whiteboard in his office, listing the very few investment models he believed in. Costco was his best example of one of them. Scale efficiencies shared. Most companies pursue scale efficiencies, he wrote, but few share them.

o33.say: And he spotted the paradox at its heart. The company grows by giving more back. Ask most companies what they'd do with windfall profits, and they'll spend it, or return it to shareholders. Almost no one replies, give it back to customers. That, he wrote, is why competing with Costco is so hard.

o41.say: So why was the stock cheap? Wall Street saw three problems. Low margins. Costco kept just one point seven cents of every sales dollar as profit, against three point six at Wal-Mart, and four point two at Target. It looked expensive, at twenty four times earnings. And costs were rising.

o42.say: Sleep turned each one around. Low margins? That's the point. Costco defers profit today, to extend the life of the franchise. Expensive? If it simply raised prices to Wal-Mart's margins, it would trade at about eleven times earnings. But would it be a better business? We think not, he wrote.

o43.say: The share price had fallen from a high of fifty five dollars in two thousand, to about thirty, where Nomad bought. Sleep called Costco as perfect a growth stock as we have analysed, available at close to half price.

o44.say: And there's a twist. One famous investor, a man Sleep called an industry hero, owned Costco, but kept it to just one percent of his fund. He said labour and customers were getting too much of the rewards. Sleep disagreed. Our investment hero was mistaken, he wrote, by about twenty dollars a share so far.

o45.say: Sleep was just as hard on himself. He'd started with only about three percent of the fund in Costco. Already, he wrote, your manager may have made his first mistake investing in Costco. From not buying enough.

o51.say: Then Sleep invented a way to measure this kind of moat. He called it the robustness ratio. How much does the customer save, for every dollar the company keeps?

o52.say: Remember case file one? Sleep used GEICO. Its customers saved about a billion dollars against the next cheapest insurer. And GEICO earned about a billion. One dollar saved, for every dollar kept. At Costco, he estimated five dollars saved for customers, for every dollar the company kept.

o53.say: He even did the shopping maths. A typical cardholder spent about eleven hundred dollars a year at Costco, saving around a hundred and seventy five dollars, for a fee of about twenty three dollars. Look around you, he wrote. How many companies save five dollars for their customers, for every one dollar they keep?

o61.say: So was it a moat, or charity? By two thousand five, Costco was Nomad's largest holding. Sleep explained why. Costco's obsession with sharing made its future more predictable, and less risky, than the average business.

o62.say: In twenty ten, Sleep found where the low costs really came from. Not cheap land. Not cheap wages. From a thousand daily decisions to save money, made by a hundred and forty seven thousand employees, across five hundred and sixty six warehouses.

o63.say: And then, mid sentence, Jim Sinegal jumped up and pulled out an old memo from nineteen sixty seven, written by Sol Price, the founder of Fed-Mart, the company Costco's story grew out of. Sleep framed a copy on his office wall. Its key line? Let us concentrate on how cheap we can bring things to the people, rather than how much the traffic will bear.

o64.say: Forty three years after that memo, Sleep noted, Costco had become the most valuable retailer of its type in the world. And when Nomad wound down, Costco was still in the portfolio. Sleep called it one of the two grandparents, along with Berkshire Hathaway.

o71.say: Now the defence. One. Thin margins leave very little room for mistakes. Two. The contract lives only as long as management resists temptation. One greedy boss, and it's gone. Three. Sleep himself warned that a low share price could invite a buyout at a bad price. And four. This kind of culture is very hard to build later. It usually has to be there from day one.

o72.say: So, here's our verdict. The Costco moat is scale efficiencies shared, and a customer who trusts that the markup will never secretly change. Its biggest threat is the temptation to take a little more. And its status? Nomad's biggest bet, and still held when the partnership closed.

o80.say: When you study any Indian company that claims to give customers the best value, open a case file with three questions.

o81.say: One. When its costs fall, do its prices fall too? Two. Roughly how much does a customer save, for every rupee the company keeps? Three. If it had a windfall, would management give some back to customers?

o82.say: We're not saying any Indian company has this moat. You do the detective work.

o83.say: One line for your friend over chai. The shop that shares its savings, keeps its customers.

o84.say: Every clue here comes from Nick Sleep's letters to his partners. The sources are in the description.

o85.say: Next case. A store chain that looked expensive for forty years, and kept getting sold too early by smart investors. How do you value a moat that keeps growing? Case file nine. Subscribe, and I'll see you at the crime scene.
